analysis.one_liner: Forces tobacco companies to sharply cut the number of children who use their products, with fines if they fail.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House committee from June 1997 until Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the government to survey every year how many children use each tobacco company's products. Each company would have had to cut that number steadily, down to 10% of its starting level within six years. Any company that missed the targets would pay a fee on every unit of tobacco it sold, with the first $1 billion a year going to enforcement and campaigns to keep kids from smoking.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, who would face fewer tobacco products marketed and sold in ways that reach them, and taxpayers, who would get funding for enforcement and youth anti-smoking programs at the tobacco companies' expense. State and local governments would also keep full freedom to pass their own stricter youth-tobacco rules, since the bill explicitly does not override them.

how_it_helps.text: Each tobacco manufacturer must cut the number of children using its products to 80% of its baseline after two years, 60% after three, 40% after four, 20% after five, and 10% or less after six [S3].
Companies that miss the targets pay a noncompliance fee of $1 per unit sold, rising by $1 per unit for each consecutive year of failure, with modest credit for near-compliance [S3].

The first $1 billion in fees each year funds a Tobacco Enforcement and Education Fund for federal tobacco enforcement and public education to discourage children from smoking; anything above that goes to the Treasury [S3].
The bill does not preempt any federal, state, or local law that reduces children's tobacco use, so stricter local rules would remain in force [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, which would face federally mandated reductions in child customers and escalating per-unit fees if they failed. Some of those fees would likely be passed through to adult smokers in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill's enforcement hinge is an annual government survey of which children used which company's products, so penalties depend on survey accuracy and could be disputed even though judicial review is limited to one court and only after the fee is paid [S3].
Fees charged on every unit distributed would raise costs across the board, meaning adult smokers — many of them lower-income — would help pay even when the target is youth use [S3].
Tying penalties to a shrinking base of youth users could create pressure to redefine or game the survey measure rather than genuinely reduce smoking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real public-health leverage — money and mandated reductions aimed directly at the companies whose products reach children — bought with an imperfect survey-based enforcement mechanism and costs that spill onto adult smokers through pass-through pricing. The design is aggressive but coherent; the main uncertainty is whether survey-based measurement could withstand years of challenge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1997, referred to the House Commerce Committee, sent to its health subcommittee two weeks later, and never moved again before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the NO Tobacco for Kids Act in the House on June 3, 1997 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced [S1].
On June 18, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment — the last action of any kind in its two-year life [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any further action before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: for the entire 105th Congress they faced no federally mandated reduction targets for child customers and no per-unit penalty tied to youth use. The bill died without any record vote, so no member ever had to go on record on it.

for.name: Rep. Henry A. Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Five House cosponsors (1 Republican, 4 Democrats)
for.role: Cosponsors including Reps. Hansen (R-UT) and Meehan (D-MA)

against.name: House Committee on Commerce (Chair Thomas J. Bliley Jr.)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican from Virginia
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or advanced it out of committee in two years.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers of cigarettes and smokeless tobacco
against.what_they_did: The bill targeted them with mandated child-use reductions and per-unit penalties; no industry lobbying activity appears in the congressional record for this bill, though the industry was a major lobbying presence in Congress during the 1997-98 tobacco debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a small bipartisan bench — a Democratic lead sponsor plus five cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 1 Republican — but it never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have made each company legally responsible for cutting the number of children using its products by 90% over six years, with $1-per-unit fees escalating for repeat failures — a direct hit to youth-driven sales and a liability framework the industry had no incentive to accept. Companies that failed would effectively be paying customers' way into an enforcement and education fund. Its interest ran against the bill's public-health purpose.
